description: We are a team of three enthusiastic engineering students passionate about space, innovation, and problem-solving. We enjoy learning, exploring new ideas, and working together. We are looking for creative and motivated teammates with skills in coding, research, design, data analysis, or storytelling. Let's collaborate and create something amazing! 🚀
summary:
AgroSat v7 is a satellite-based agricultural decision-support system designed to help farmers make sustainable and informed crop-selection decisions. It integrates satellite imagery, weather data, soil characteristics, and climatic conditions to recommend suitable crops for three agricultural seasons: Kharif, Rabi, and Zaid.
The system uses technologies such as NASA POWER, MODIS NDVI, ISRIC SoilGrids, SRTM, and USDA datasets to analyse rainfall, temperature, soil moisture, vegetation health, and soil properties. It evaluates 18 crops based on water requirements, cultivation costs, profitability, drought tolerance, and soil suitability.
AgroSat also provides crop rotation planning, climate stress analysis, satellite-based vegetation monitoring, and comparison of farming strategies. Developed using Python Flask, HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Leaflet, and Chart.js, the application aims to improve water management, soil health, agricultural productivity, and climate resilience through data-driven recommendations.
details:
AgroSat: Project Details

What it does and how it works

AgroSat is a web app that helps farmers choose crop rotations using NASA Earth observations. A farmer sets their location by GPS or by typing a village, town or district name. They then tell us their water availability, budget, current crop and up to three ranked priorities, such as saving water, keeping costs low, earning more or improving soil.

AgroSat pulls NASA POWER climate, MODIS vegetation history (NDVI), SRTM terrain, NASA GIBS map layers and SMAP/IMERG pass information for that exact spot. It also detects soil type using ISRIC SoilGrids, and in the US adds USDA SSURGO, the Cropland Data Layer and PRISM climate normals.

The app scores each crop for each season on climate, soil and water fit, then steers the ranking by the farmer's priorities. It compares four rotations: the farmer's current one, one built from their priorities, a water saver and a soil builder. Each shows why it was suggested, the evidence, benefits, information gaps and risks for local review. Scores come with ranges and a confidence level, and sliders let the farmer test hotter, drier or wetter weather.

Benefits

  • Farmers get clear advice without needing GIS or satellite skills.
  • Rotations are compared honestly, including the bare-field seasons of the current system.
  • Planning for water, soil, erosion and pests is built in.
  • The tool shows its evidence, gaps and uncertainty instead of giving a bare answer.

Intended impact

We want to help farmers make more resilient choices: using less water, protecting soil from erosion, and breaking pest cycles. It is meant to support farmer judgment, not replace local agricultural experts. We also want to show that open NASA data can reach smallholder farmers in plain language.

Tools and technology

  • Languages: Python and JavaScript, with HTML and CSS.
  • Backend: Flask, with parallel calls to the data services.
  • Frontend: vanilla JavaScript, Leaflet maps and Chart.js.
  • Data: NASA POWER, MODIS (via ORNL DAAC), SRTM, NASA GIBS, NASA CMR, ISRIC SoilGrids, USDA SSURGO, CDL, PRISM and OpenStreetMap.
  • Development: VS Code, Git and GitHub. We also used an AI assistant (Claude) for coding help. [Edit this line to match your team's AI-use disclosure.]
  • Hardware: no special hardware. It runs on an ordinary laptop in a browser.

What is creative

  • Farmers pick a place by name or GPS instead of typing coordinates.
  • Their ranked priorities change the recommendation.
  • We use NASA Harvest GLAM's crop-condition method at the farmer's exact point, and stress detected from satellites shifts the ranking toward drought-tolerant crops.
  • Strategies show their uncertainty and risks openly, and weather sliders let farmers explore "what if" scenarios.
  • It has a dark, modern interface and a plain-language guide to terms like evapotranspiration and NDVI.

What we considered

  • Farmers first: simple language, minimal typing, and clear reminders to confirm with local experts.
  • Honesty about data: every source is labelled live or planned, and information gaps are listed for each strategy.
  • Privacy and security: API keys are stored only on the server and never sent to the browser.
  • Reliability: each data service fails on its own, so one outage doesn't stop the app.
  • Limitations: crop traits are generic estimates, soil outside the US comes from a 250 m model, and market prices and machinery limits are not yet included.

Honest status

The app is built, but we have not yet run every live data service end to end, and datasets such as SMAP values, ECOSTRESS and GRACE are planned. Before submitting, test it with real coordinates and update any lines to match what you see working.
